reason: The statement captures the court's probate holding that the propounder must satisfy the court that the will is the act of a capable testator.
The court applied the rule that suspicious circumstances must be removed before probate can be granted.
The case held that unpaid acquired-land owners satisfying section 21 became statutory lessees, not the broad compensation proposition stated.
The court held that satisfaction of section 21(1) made the owner a statutory lessee irrespective of the extent owned.
The statement omits the statutory limit that alienation is the maximum permissible extent or the extent actually acquired, whichever is less.
The court held the later action was not barred because the media of title differed, so the statement reverses the effect of the holding.
The court held that prescription had to be reconsidered in the plaintiff's new character as transferee from Jefferjee.
The court upheld the specific appointments in this temple succession, not a general rule that appointment by deed is always valid.
The prior cases were maintenance actions and the present action was a status claim, so the statement misstates the res judicata reasoning.
Estoppel was a holding, but this formulation is too generic and omits the represented conduct and prior litigation context.
The statement is directionally right but drops the material qualification that the correction power was for an accidental slip or omission.
The statement is too vague to reflect the holding about the limited prohibitory order available under section 69(2).
The quote supports the holding that entitlement to a non-possessory land right is declared only subject to final determination by a competent court.
The court held that dismissing on an uncontested lis pendens point without hearing parties violated natural justice.
The court held the lis pendens was correctly registered in the folios of the deeds for the land described in the plaint.
The statement omits the material requirement that the judge choose among specified courses only after hearing the parties.
The court treated the notary's two signatures as part of the attestation scheme needed to decide the validity of the protected-holding transfer.
The definition of cause of action in section 5 of the Civil Procedure Code was central to rejecting the objection to amendment.
The statement gives one amendment rule but omits the paired limitation that an amendment causing injustice should not be allowed.
The court adopted the rule that amendments working injustice to the other side should not be allowed.
The statement is supported but omits that the vested right was only to evaluation under the announced promotion criteria, not promotion itself.
A declaration was appropriate in this contractual-right context, but the statement is overbroad without that qualification and the mandamus contrast.
The court held that Rent Act protected tenancies survive a partition decree or certificate of sale even if not reserved in the partition decree.
The statement is malformed and fails to state the actual section 52(2)(b) and Rent Act protection rule for lawful sub-tenants.
The court held that pleading value does not affect recoverable partition costs, which are based on appraised value under section 57.
